headline: Iran denies Hormuz talks, pushing oil above $84 and rate-cut hopes lower
tldr: Iran's foreign minister flatly denies any direct US talks, contradicting Washington and pushing Brent above $84 a barrel.
Fed funds futures now price rates at 4% by year-end, up from the current 3.50–3.75% hold, pressuring US equities.
Houthis struck a Saudi Aramco refinery and Red Sea port, killing seven, raising shipping-route risk further.
UK GDP expected to show 0.4% growth in Q2; June monthly figure could be flat or slightly negative.
FPL deadline is Friday 17:30 BST — Šeško flagged as likely available, Martínez confirmed out for Arsenal opener.

sections.title: Markets
sections.body:
**Markets — Tuesday 11 August 2026**

The single biggest driver right now is the Hormuz–Fed double bind. 
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated Tehran is not currently in direct talks with the US to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz — directly contradicting Washington's earlier assertion that a deal is near.
 That denial has a mechanical consequence: 
oil rose on Monday as traders reassessed whether any deal is imminent, with Brent gaining over 1% to above $84 a barrel.
 
Westpac noted that "uncertainty remains high as we go into the sixth month of the Iran war," with the strait still effectively closed and Houthis disrupting Red Sea alternatives.


Higher oil feeds directly into rate expectations. 
The Iran conflict's energy-price shock has shifted market expectations from 2026 rate cuts toward possible rate hikes.
 
The FOMC held at 3.50–3.75% at its 29 July meeting
, but 
fed funds futures are now pricing the rate at 4% by year end.
 That repricing is the ceiling over equities currently sitting near record multiples.

US indices drifted lower on Monday as a result. 
The Dow fell 0.31% to 53,869, the Nasdaq dropped 0.28%, and the S&P 500 slipped 0.07% to 7,751.
 
Nvidia fell nearly 3%, weighing on major indices, following a Financial Times report it is working with Apollo Global and Blackstone on a $500bn AI infrastructure funding package
 — investors read the scale of that fundraise as a sign of capital strain rather than confidence. 
Asian stocks are set for a muted open today, ahead of key US inflation prints
 that could reset the rate narrative entirely — CPI data this week is the next hard catalyst.

European markets are holding up better. 
The Stoxx 600 traded broadly flat on Monday, just below its all-time high after its strongest weekly advance since late June; the DAX, CAC 40, and FTSE 100 were largely unchanged.
 
The Stoxx 600 recorded its fourth consecutive record close last Friday, with gains broad-based across Germany, France, London, and Italy — technology shares were the standout sector, tracking Wall Street's exuberance.


**In Sam's portfolio:** AMD's -2.85% is consistent with the Nvidia-led tech pullback — end-demand sentiment deteriorating. ASML's -0.43% is a milder move for the same reason; as equipment infrastructure it has a partial buffer. The defence names are the bright spot: QinetiQ +1.81%, Chemring +1.75%, BAE +1.08%, and WDEF +0.65% — all benefiting from the same geopolitical tension that's hurting broader risk assets.

**Watch:** US CPI (due this week) is the swing factor. A hot print would validate futures pricing of 4% Fed funds by year-end and reprice equities down; a soft one reopens the pause-and-hold narrative and likely bounces tech.

sections.title: Fantasy Premier League
sections.body:
**Deadline: Friday 21 Aug, 17:30 BST — 3 days away**

**Prices**


Prices remain locked until the GW1 deadline; the market opens after that.
 Nothing to chase today — squad finalisation is the priority.

**Injuries — what's new since yesterday**

Two meaningful updates from the pre-fetched flags and press conference reporting:

- **Šeško (Man Utd, £X, 2.4% owned)** — 
Amorim says Šeško is "ready to play" but wouldn't confirm whether he will start.
 That's a meaningful step up from yesterday's bare "75% chance" flag — he's in the squad conversation, at minimum.
- **Martínez (Man Utd)** — 
Lisandro Martínez is out injured
, confirmed by Amorim ahead of the Arsenal opener. Avoids United's defensive assets accordingly.
- **Kroupi Jr (Bournemouth, 3.5% owned)** — foot injury, unknown return. 
Among the clearest current avoids heading into GW1.

- **Chalobah / Digne** — both now permanent departures (Como and PSG respectively), per pre-fetched data. If either is in your squad, move them out before Friday.

**Differentials**


Havertz is the standout differential pick for GW1, sitting at just 6.9% ownership.
 
He and Mateta project as season-long differentials rather than one-week punts, with a combination of top-tier xGI/90 and reasonable fixture ease.
 
Ngumoha is the highest-variance play — use him as a GW1 flier with an exit plan if he doesn't start, rather than a set-and-forget pick.


On fixtures, 
Sunderland's opening two gameweeks — Ipswich away, then Fulham at home — make their assets viable differential options for adventurous managers,
 though Mukiele and Alderete both carry knock uncertainty (75% chance of playing per pre-fetched data).

sections.title: Data & BI
sections.body:
Two genuine developments to flag today — one from BigQuery (published this week) and one service-level Power BI change taking effect now.

---

**BigQuery: performance optimisations blog and DTS Iceberg support**


Google published a post on 7 August addressing query performance tuning in BigQuery, noting the growing challenge as agentic workloads increase the volume and variety of queries hitting the warehouse.
 Separately, 
BigQuery Data Transfer Service now supports direct ingestion into Apache Iceberg managed tables in preview — covering sources including GCS, Amazon S3, and Azure Blob Storage, published 8 August.
 For teams running open lakehouse architectures, this removes a step: data lands natively in Iceberg format rather than requiring a post-load conversion.

**Power BI: semantic model settings pane goes live in August**

Beyond the July feature summary items already covered, there is one rollout happening right now: 
starting in August, opening settings for a semantic model in the Power BI Service takes you to the new settings *pane* rather than the full settings page — it opens beside your content rather than replacing the view.
 Minor UX change, but worth knowing if you have support docs or training material that includes screenshots of the old full-page settings layout.

**dbt Summit (fka Coalesce) — early-bird deadline this week**

Practical note: 
dbt Summit runs 15–18 September in Las Vegas, with standard registration at $1,695 until 17 August — last-chance pricing of $1,895 kicks in from the 18th.
 If anyone on the team is planning to attend, this week is the cut-off.

sections.title: Career & Data Leadership
sections.body:
**Salary benchmarks — fresh numbers**


Head of Data and data management leadership roles in the UK frequently exceed £90,000, particularly where responsibility spans governance, reporting strategy, and enterprise data architecture.
 
Across data, AI, and cybersecurity, salaries are rising by up to 6% — roughly double the 2–4% average across the wider market
, per [Digital Waffle](https://www.digitalwaffle.co/salary-guides). 
The specific pinch point is a scarcity of digital expertise at leadership level, driving sharply competitive packages for senior AI, Cloud, and Data hires.


For role-level context on live listings: 
Head of Data & BI roles outside London are currently advertising around £90–95k (York, hybrid), while London Head of Platform / AI & Data roles are reaching £120k.


**What hirers are actually asking for**

The job spec language is shifting. 
Head of Data Engineering roles now routinely require candidates to own architectural strategy *and* sit at the intersection of technical delivery and business outcomes, reporting into Director of Data Monetisation and working up to C-suite.
 
The top stated priority from hiring organisations is demonstrating tangible value — executive teams are demanding data initiatives directly support growth, efficiency, and resilience.


**Leadership lens — what's new**

Yesterday covered the "fix foundations before outputs" framing. A complementary signal worth adding: 
the governance failure mode that gets noticed at board level is leadership spending meeting time validating numbers rather than evaluating options
 — that's the diagnostic question to put to an interviewer. 
The talent challenge in 2026 is not just about hiring specialists; it is about enabling the broader organisation to work effectively with data and AI
 — which reframes the Head of Data role as an organisational change job as much as a technical one.

sections.title: UK Insurance
sections.body:
Most of today's search returns are either already covered in yesterday's briefing or pre-date it. The Morrisons item is from mid-June and therefore stale. The FCA priorities report is from February. The genuinely fresh angles are: (1) the FCA's claims-outsourcing review findings expected in early 2027 — a new near-term deadline; (2) the premium finance monitoring continuing under the 2026 priorities; (3) the home insurance weather/property claims pressure picture; and (4) the retail brand distribution push (Morrisons adding further texture to the supermarket trend already noted yesterday on John Lewis/IKEA). Given yesterday's section already covered motor losses, FCA simplification, John Lewis, and MGAA AI governance, there is limited genuinely new material — but there are a few distinct, fresh items worth briefly covering: the FCA's outsourced claims oversight review (outcome due early 2027), the premium finance monitoring angle, and the broader supermarket insurance distribution acceleration as a named trend with Morrisons adding context.

---

**Retail brands: the supermarket distribution push deepens**

Yesterday flagged John Lewis Money and IKEA/Urban Jungle. The wider pattern is sharper than those two examples suggest. 
UK supermarket insurance expansion has accelerated sharply in 2025 and 2026, with each major grocer now treating insurance as a core component of its financial services proposition.
 
Hood Group has partnered with Morrisons to launch pet and travel insurance, with pet cover underwritten by Burns & Wilcox/Accredited Insurance (UK) and travel underwritten by AXA.
 
Loyalty does the heavy lifting: new pet policyholders earn 20,000 More Card points; travel buyers get 10% off.
 The loyalty-linked model is worth watching — it makes switching cost-sticky in a way that price-comparison aggregators cannot easily replicate.

**FCA: claims outsourcing review incoming**


The FCA's regulatory priorities confirm it is reviewing consumer understanding, claims-handling outcomes, and insurers' oversight of outsourced and delegated-authority arrangements — with findings expected in early 2027.
 That gives personal lines teams roughly two to three reporting cycles to get their third-party oversight evidence in order before the regulator publishes.

**Premium finance: still on the watch list**


Premium finance remains an area of FCA attention following its recent market study; while the FCA notes cost reductions since 2022, it will continue to monitor APRs and act where fair value concerns persist.
 With motor premiums rising again, the proportion of customers financing premiums is likely to tick up — keeping this firmly in scope.

sections.title: Milton Keynes
sections.body:
**Events — diary these**

- **📅 4 Aug** — [Code for Her](https://protospace.uk/events) coding academy and forum for women, at Aiimi HQ, 18:30–20:30. Tonight — short notice, but worth knowing it's on.

- **📅 25 Aug** — 
[NatWest Tech Tuesdays](https://protospace.uk/events) networking at NatWest Community Hub, 11:30–13:00.


- **📅 12–16 Oct** — 
**MK Tech Week 2026.** Running 12–16 October, the week culminates in a one-day conference and expo at Unity Place on 15 October, themed around **"Sovereign Technology"** — how the UK develops and protects critical technologies, data and digital infrastructure.
 
Partners span government, education and industry, including The Open University, MK:U, HMGCC, BSI, Serve Robotics and Bletchley Park.
 The sovereign tech angle makes this directly relevant for a senior data professional — expect sessions on data infrastructure, national security and AI governance. Register interest at [miltonkeynestechweek.com](https://miltonkeynestechweek.com).

- **📅 17 Sept** — 
TNMOC/London Mathematical Society Conference at Bletchley Park, 10:00–17:30.
 Niche but high-quality; worth a look if formal tech history or maths-adjacent research is of interest.

- **📅 14 Oct** — 
[MK Cyber Social Event](https://protospace.uk/events) at Warbler on the Wharf, Campbell Wharf Marina, 18:00–21:00.
 Good informal touchpoint immediately after Tech Week.

**Local news**

- **Council Plan 2026/27.** 
MKCC has published its Council Plan for 2026/27 with 70 action points, building on an LGA independent review that called it "well run and high performing."
 
Actions include fixing potholes, building affordable homes, and investing in health centres.
 Workmanlike rather than transformative, but sets the political context for planning decisions this year.

- **UKRI Innovation Circuit.** 
UKRI has committed up to £20 million to support The Open University-led Innovation Circuit project
 — strengthening MK's position within the Oxford–Cambridge Growth Corridor and likely to influence future tech hiring and research partnerships locally.

sections.title: News
sections.body:
I'll search across several angles simultaneously to get a broad spread of fresh headlines.
Here is today's News section:

---

**Gaza — Netanyahu doubles down.** Yesterday's briefing covered the initial rejection of Trump's 15-point plan. The story has since hardened: 
Netanyahu described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House" but made clear he was willing to challenge him.
 The public defiance is now straining the bilateral relationship more explicitly than before.

**Hormuz talks stall.** 
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says there are no direct talks with the US and insists the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until Washington meets Tehran's key demands.
 
Details of a potential Iran-Oman deal emerged, but Tehran suggested vessels linked to "hostile countries" would be barred
 — a condition that makes any agreement commercially meaningless for the West.

**Yemen escalation.** 
The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi Aramco's refinery in Jazan and the Red Sea port of Mocha
, 
killing at least seven people and wounding around 30.
 Shipping-route risk is rising again.

**UK — GDP watch.** 
Economists expect official figures this week to show UK GDP grew around 0.4% between April and June, following 0.6% growth in Q1.
 
Forecasts for June's monthly figure range from a 0.1% contraction to a 0.1% increase, with households and businesses potentially turning more cautious ahead of the autumn Budget.


**Assam flooding.** 
Days of heavy monsoon rain have caused rivers, including the Brahmaputra, to overflow, inundating communities and damaging infrastructure
 across north-east India — a slow-moving humanitarian story worth watching given supply-chain implications.
